title: Count the Expressions That Reach the Target
statement:
`digits` is a text of digits. Between every two neighbouring digits you may put **nothing** (so the digits join into one longer number), a `+`, a `-` or a `*`. This gives an arithmetic expression, evaluated with the usual rule that `*` is done before `+` and `-`.

A number inside an expression must not have a **leading zero** (`05` is not allowed, but a lone `0` is). Count the expressions whose value is exactly `target`.
constraints: digits contains only the characters 0 to 9

hints.nudge: A multiplication binds tighter than the addition before it. How can you evaluate the expression while you build it, without a separate evaluator?
hints.pattern: Backtracking that keeps the value so far AND the last term (the part that a following `*` would multiply); on `*` take the last term back out of the value and put the product in.
hints.walkthrough: There are at most 4^8 = 65,536 ways to choose the operators for 9 digits, so a complete search is fine; the difficulty is evaluating each expression correctly. Instead of building a string and evaluating it, carry two numbers through the recursion: `value`, the value of the expression so far, and `last`, the last term that was added or subtracted (for `-` it is the negated number). A new `+` or `-` simply adds or subtracts the new number to the value and the new number becomes the last term. A `*` must multiply the LAST TERM, not the whole value: undo it (value - last) and add the product (last * num); the last term becomes last * num, so that another `*` after it keeps working. The first number has no operator in front of it. Reject numbers with leading zeros: once a part starts with `0` it can only be that single digit. Use 64-bit numbers, the products can be large.
